title: Ultrastructural Mastery: Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM) in Clinical Practice
summary: Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM) is the gold-standard high-frequency imaging modality (35–50 MHz) for visualizing the anterior segment structures in exquisite, cross-sectional detail. It allows for definitive assessment of the iris, ciliary body, and angle anatomy, even in the presence of significant corneal opacity.

sections.title: Technical Principles & Physics
sections.content: UBM utilizes high-frequency (35-50 MHz) transducers providing high spatial resolution (approx. 25-50 μm) at the expense of tissue penetration (depth of 5-8 mm). This allows detailed visualization of structures posterior to the iris, which are inaccessible to light-based imaging (OCT) in opaque media.

sections.title: Clinical Red Flags for UBM Referral
content: Unexplained elevated IOP with closed angle on gonioscopy
Suspected ciliary body melanoma or cyst
Post-traumatic suspicion of ciliary body dialysis or foreign body
Anterior capsule contraction syndrome with zonular instability

sections.title: Examination Protocol
content: Step 2: Placement of scleral immersion cup (e.g., ClearScan or internal eye cup).
Step 3: Fill cup with coupling medium (Methylcellulose or saline).
Step 4: Align transducer perpendicular to the limbus for radial/transverse scans.
Step 5: Dynamic assessment during light vs. dark and accommodation.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform in both light and dark to assess pupil-block dynamics.
Use 360-degree radial scans to look for ciliary body effusions or 'kissing' choroidals.
Crucial for identifying 'ciliary sulcus' positioning of IOL haptics.
Look for the 'double hump' sign in plateau iris syndrome.
Distinguish between appositional and synechial angle closure.

sections.title: Incidence of Pathology in Angle Assessment
Recent Advances
sections.content: Recent integration of 3D UBM reconstruction software and AI-based angle quantification tools have enhanced reproducibility. Studies by Pavlin and Foster remain the cornerstone of UBM interpretation, while newer high-speed digital processors reduce motion artifact in pediatric populations.
